cells.quote: The learning curves of LS and RS demonstrate an early superiority of RS, with inflexion at round six for both modalities and a leveling off at similar scores at round 10, as seen in Fig. 3.
cells.note: Robotic simulation was initially superior, but both modalities showed similar inflexion and leveling-off points.

D.comparison: English and maths attainment genetic associations

O.outcome_detail: standardised national subject tests at ages 11 and 14

cells.quote: Across the three GWAS we identified one genome-wide significant SNP association for attainment in science (rs9529641, p = 4.86 × 10–8) (Fig. 1, see also Supplementary Fig. S1A and Supplementary Table S2), but none for attainment in English or maths (Supplementary Fig. S1B–C).
cells.note: Genetic association study; the comparison is subject specificity, not a randomized treatment.

D.comparison: variance shared with other academic subjects or IQ removed

O.outcome_detail: SNP-based heritability of adolescent science attainment

result.effect: h2SNP = 0.13 after controlling for other subjects; 0.15 after controlling for IQ

cells.quote: LDSC-based h2SNP estimates were lower than in the original analyses, but still significantly larger than 0 for AA-regressed and IQ-regressed science and maths scores (p′s < 0.05) (Table 4).
cells.note: The text supports residual genetic variance after statistical adjustment, not an instructional effect.

O.outcome_detail: specificity of SNP associations with adolescent subject attainment

cells.quote: Using a z-test we were able to show that rs9529641 is significantly more associated with science than English (z = 2.48, p = 0.01) but not maths (z = 1.06, p = 0.14).
cells.note: The study compares genetic associations rather than manipulating instruction or learning conditions.
